blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Multimodal contrastive learning models such as CLIP are vulnerable to backdoor attacks with diverse trigger structures, ranging from localized patches to globally distributed perturbations, with recent attacks increasingly optimizing these triggers in the representation space. Existing post-hoc defenses based on clean fine-tuning may leave backdoors active, while trigger-inversion methods depend on accurately estimating the attack target and trigger. We observe that backdoored encoders exhibit structure-dependent representation sensitivity: global perturbations preferentially expose distributed backdoors, whereas local patch perturbations are more effective for localized backdoors. Based on this observation, we propose Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense (GARD), a target- and trigger-agnostic post-hoc defense. GARD optimizes complementary global and local adversarial probes to maximally displace clean-image representations, and then realigns the perturbed representations with detached clean anchors while preserving image-text alignment. The resulting model requires no additional computation at inference time. Across six visual backdoor attacks and two CLIP visual backbones, GARD reduces the attack success rate below 1% in all 12 evaluated attack-backbone combinations while maintaining competitive clean accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of adversarial representation probing for repairing backdoored multimodal contrastive encoders.
blocks.zh: CLIP等多式对比式学习模型容易被有多种触发结构的后门攻击所伤害,从局部补丁到全球分布的扰动不等,最近的攻击越来越优化了在表示空间中的这些触发. 现有的基于清洁微调的后热防御可能使后门活动,而触发反转方法则依赖于准确估计攻击目标和触发. 我们注意到后门编码器表现出结构依赖性的代表敏感性:全球扰动偏好暴露分布式后门,而局部补丁扰动则对局部后门更有效. 基于这一观察,我们提出"渐入-引导"的反面代表防御(GARD),即目标-和触发-不可知的后危险防御. GARD优化了互为补充的全球和地方对抗探测器,以最大程度地取代了清洁图像的表示,然后在保持图像文本对齐的同时,用脱开的清洁锚来调整被扰动的表示. 由此产生的模型在推论时不需要额外的计算. 在六个视觉后门攻击和两个CLIP视觉骨干中,GARD将攻击成功率降低到所有12个被评价的攻击后骨组合的1%以下,同时保持竞争性的清洁精度. 这些结果表明,对抗性代表测试对于修理后门多式对比编码器是有效的。

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Multimodal contrastive learning (MCL) models, such as CLIP, have demonstrated
remarkable capabilities in learning transferable visual representations by
aligning images and texts in a shared embedding space [ 23 , 14 ] .
These pretrained models have become essential components in many downstream
vision–language applications [ 22 , 21 , 3 , 5 , 8 , 17 ] , where their reliability and security are
increasingly important. However, recent studies have shown that MCL models are
vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where an attacker can implant hidden behaviors
during training such that images containing specific triggers are associated
with attacker-defined concepts while maintaining normal performance on clean
samples [ 15 , 1 ] . Unlike conventional
backdoors in classification models that primarily manipulate decision
boundaries, backdoors in MCL models compromise the semantic alignment between
visual and textual representations, creating new challenges for model
purification.

blocks.en:
Existing defenses against backdoored MCL models mainly follow two paradigms:
clean-data-based purification and trigger-oriented recovery. Clean fine-tuning
methods attempt to restore benign image–text alignment using clean
data [ 1 ] , but they provide limited supervision on
trigger-induced behaviors and may fail to remove hidden backdoor associations.
Trigger inversion methods instead exploit adversarial behaviors to estimate
attack targets or recover trigger patterns before
purification [ 26 ] . However, their effectiveness relies on
accurate target estimation and assumptions about the trigger structure. This
limitation becomes increasingly significant as recent attacks move beyond
handcrafted patterns toward optimized triggers with diverse spatial
structures, including localized patches and globally distributed
perturbations. Therefore, developing a defense strategy that does not rely on
specific knowledge of the attack remains an important challenge.

Recent observations on the connection between adversarial behaviors and
backdoor attacks suggest that compromised models may contain abnormal
sensitivity patterns that can be exploited without directly observing the
original trigger [ 26 ] . This motivates us to revisit the

itself, an alternative direction is to identify the representation
vulnerabilities that enable different triggers to manipulate the learned
semantic space. Since backdoor attacks ultimately alter image representations
toward attacker-specified semantics, these vulnerabilities may provide a more
general defense target than the trigger patterns in the input space.

To investigate this possibility, we first study whether backdoored MCL models
exhibit structure-dependent representation vulnerabilities. Our analysis
reveals that different trigger structures produce distinct adversarial
sensitivity patterns: globally distributed backdoors are more effectively
exposed by global perturbations, whereas localized triggers are better revealed
through local perturbation probes. More importantly, such vulnerabilities can
be identified without access to the original trigger or attack target,
suggesting that adversarial perturbations can serve as a trigger-agnostic
mechanism for probing backdoor behaviors.

Based on these observations, we propose Gradient-Guided Adversarial
Representation Defense (GARD), a trigger- and target-agnostic defense for
MCL models. As illustrated in Figure 1 , GARD
alternates between adversarial probing and representation realignment. It
constructs complementary global and local adversarial views to cover distributed and
spatially concentrated input variations, respectively, and realigns their
representations with a detached clean-image anchor while preserving clean
image–text correspondence. This alternating procedure requires neither the
true trigger nor its target, and introduces no additional computation at
inference time.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
The shared embedding space of MCL models creates a
distinct attack surface: a small set of poisoned image–text pairs can associate
an image trigger with an attacker-chosen textual concept. Early studies showed
that such associations can survive transfer to downstream tasks and zero-shot
classifiers [ 15 , 1 ] . Recent attacks make
this association harder to remove by optimizing the trigger itself. BadCLIP
jointly guides the visual trigger with target-side visual and textual
embeddings, so that triggered samples approach the target semantics in both
modalities [ 18 ] . BadVision instead compromises a reusable
vision encoder using an imperceptible, globally distributed perturbation
optimized toward a target representation, and further trains the encoder to
distinguish the valid trigger from unrelated adversarial noise [ 19 ] . These developments expand the trigger space from
fixed patches and blending patterns to optimized local or distributed
perturbations. They also motivate defenses that do not assume a particular
trigger geometry.

blocks.en:
Existing defenses intervene through detection, pre-training, post-hoc
fine-tuning, or inference. DECREE detects compromised encoders without
repairing them [ 10 ] . SAFECLIP separates likely clean and risky image–text pairs during
pre-training and applies cross-modal learning only to the progressively
expanded safe subset [ 27 ] ; this setting presumes control over
the original training process. Post-hoc purification instead uses clean-data
fine-tuning and adversarial augmentation [ 1 , 16 ] .
The connection between adversarial perturbations
and backdoor behavior is already well recognized in backdoor defense.
InverTune exploits this connection by generating a universal adversarial
perturbation to elicit target-associated responses from the compromised model;
it then estimates the attack target, reconstructs a latent trigger, and applies
clustering-guided purification [ 26 ] . Its purification signal
nevertheless depends on target estimation and trigger inversion.
Representation-decomposition analyses further show that local
patch and global perturbation attacks affect different CLIP components, and
support component-level repair or filtering at inference [ 13 ] . In contrast, GARD is a post-hoc defense that requires
neither target estimation nor trigger recovery. Rather than treating the
adversarial–backdoor connection itself as a contribution, GARD uses
target-free adversarial optimization to probe the compromised encoder under
complementary global and local perturbation spaces, and directly realigns both
adversarial representations to clean semantic anchors.

structure-specific backdoor vulnerabilities. We use the same 256 non-target

Figure 2 shows that different types of backdoors
exhibit distinct sensitivities to different forms of adversarial
perturbations. For BadVision, the
global perturbation increases the target probability by 30.61 percentage
points over its initialization, compared with 0.03 points for the local
perturbation. The trend reverses for BadCLIP: the local perturbation produces a
3.43-point increase, compared with 0.11 points for the global perturbation.
The class-wise comparison in Figure 3 further
shows that the corresponding target response is selective relative to the
other 999 classes. These results suggest that backdoors leave a structure-dependent vulnerability
footprint in the representation space: distributed and patch-based triggers
are preferentially exposed by global and local perturbations, respectively.
This observation is also consistent with the failure of a localized
target-identification probe on globally distributed triggers. Controlled
experiments in the appendix show that this structural mismatch
causes InverTune to identify an incorrect target, which in turn severely
compromises subsequent backdoor removal.

blocks.en: 4.2 Overview of GARD

blocks.en:
As illustrated in Figure 1 , GARD mitigates backdoor
attacks in MCL models through a two-stage process: complementary global and
local adversarial probing, followed by clean-anchored representation
realignment. Since backdoor attacks are designed to preserve clean utility, an
untriggered clean image generally remains aligned with its paired text and thus
provides a reliable reference for its intended semantics. GARD treats this
clean representation as a fixed anchor and realigns the deliberately displaced
representations toward it, thereby suppressing the vulnerable directions
through which trigger-like perturbations redirect an image toward
attacker-specified semantics.

blocks.en: Table 4 validates the contribution of each training objective in GARD under the BadCLIP and BadVision attacks, which represent optimized local patch triggers and globally optimized perturbations, respectively. The Base variant, which employs only the clean cross-modal alignment objective, provides little protection, retaining ASRs of 99.90% and 73.87% on BadCLIP and BadVision, respectively. This indicates that preserving clean cross-modal alignment alone is insufficient to eliminate backdoor-induced representation deviations.

In contrast, removing the local representation alignment objective leaves the defense against BadVision largely intact (0.97%) but causes the ASR on BadCLIP to increase to 99.84%, indicating that local representation alignment is essential for suppressing patch-based triggers.

blocks.en: These observations demonstrate that the two representation alignment objectives address complementary vulnerabilities induced by different trigger patterns. blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We presented GARD, a post-hoc defense that uses adversarial perturbations to
probe and repair backdoor-induced representation vulnerabilities in
MCL models. Rather than estimating the attack target or
reconstructing an unknown trigger, GARD searches for global and local input
variations that maximally displace clean-image representations and then
realigns the perturbed representations with their clean semantic anchors.
Across six attacks and two CLIP visual backbones, GARD reduced ASR below 1 % 1\% in all evaluated settings while maintaining competitive clean
accuracy. The ablation and representation analyses further showed that the
global and local objectives address complementary vulnerabilities associated
with distributed and spatially concentrated triggers. Overall, GARD demonstrates
that identifying and suppressing backdoor-induced representation vulnerabilities
offers a practical target-free direction for defending MCL models.
